Consistency.justification: The proposal is strongly aligned with the stated AgentArcEval idea. It directly addresses compound agent architectures, autonomous multi-step behavior, nondeterminism, continuous evolution, and scenario-driven evaluation, while also supplying the requested catalogue of general agent scenarios. The methodology, experiments, and limitations are mutually coherent and reflect the gaps identified in the related-work discussion. However, some additions, including differential privacy, generalized Pareto modeling, and signed traces, are only indirectly connected to architecture evaluation and make the scope broader than the core idea. The hypothesis also attributes improved violation detection to the combined protocol even though signed-trace instrumentation primarily improves auditability and provenance rather than detection itself.

Clarity.justification: The proposal is well structured and provides concrete components, baselines, sample-size tiers, metrics, ablations, and reproducibility artifacts. Important operational concepts such as attacker observability, seedability, trace fields, and reproducible exploits are described clearly. Nevertheless, several central definitions remain underspecified. An architecture-level safety violation is not formally defined, the allocation of N across scenarios, architectures, seeds, and fidelity tiers is ambiguous, and it is unclear whether the reported event rate is conditional on adversarial sampling or intended to estimate a deployment-population rate. The relationship among adaptive search, importance sampling, hierarchical pooling, and tail estimation also needs a more explicit end-to-end description.

Novelty.justification: The principal novelty is the integration of scenario catalogues, adaptive adversaries, reproducible manifests, cryptographically signed traces, lifecycle metadata, and statistical rare-event analysis into one architecture-oriented evaluation pipeline. This combination is useful and more systematic than conventional static agent benchmarks. However, most individual ingredients are established techniques: adaptive red-teaming, seedable containers, signed audit logs, exact binomial intervals, hierarchical Bayesian models, power analysis, importance sampling, and differential privacy are not themselves new. The proposal does not identify a novel algorithm, formal evaluation theory, or uniquely defined architecture-level metric that clearly separates AgentArcEval from a carefully engineered combination of existing evaluation and auditing practices.

Soundness.justification: The proposal includes several sound practices, such as power analysis, exact intervals for low counts, prior-predictive checks, prior sensitivity analysis, Bayesian convergence diagnostics, ablations, and reproducibility checks. Its main inferential design, however, has important unresolved issues. Detection rates from an adaptive adversary and rates from static i.i.d. sampling correspond to different input distributions, so a two-proportion test does not by itself establish better estimation of real-world safety risk. Adaptive selection can invalidate ordinary p-values and confidence intervals unless the stopping, selection, and weighting mechanisms are modeled. Importance sampling is mentioned without defining the target distribution, proposal distribution, likelihood ratios, or support conditions. The hierarchical Beta-Binomial specification is incomplete, including how hyperparameters are estimated and how architecture, scenario, fidelity, seed, and version effects are represented. Multiple testing across approximately 30 scenarios and many conditions is not addressed. Generalized Pareto analysis is also insufficiently tied to a well-defined continuous severity or loss variable and is not naturally applicable to binary violation indicators alone. Finally, fixed seeds do not guarantee deterministic execution on all model APIs or hardware. These issues do not make the project invalid, but they substantially limit the rigor of the proposed causal and statistical conclusions.

Feasibility.justification: Most components can be implemented with current software and statistical tools, and the proposal offers practical artifacts such as a Python SDK, containerized attack oracles, manifests, and rerun scripts. A limited pilot with two agent architectures and a subset of scenarios is realistic. The complete experimental matrix is much more demanding: roughly 30 scenarios multiplied by three fidelity tiers, four baselines, three sample-size tiers, multiple decoding settings, at least three seeds, two architectures, ablations, versions, and privacy settings could require very large numbers of costly agent and tool interactions. Live-tool experiments also create changing external state, rate limits, safety concerns, and weak replayability. Reproducing each exploit in at least 80 percent of reruns may conflict with the stated focus on rare nondeterministic failures. Feasibility would improve with an explicit budget, staged scenario selection, matched query or compute budgets, and a smaller preregistered confirmatory experiment.

Significance.justification: Evaluating foundation-model-based agents at the architecture and system level is an important safety and reliability problem. Static task benchmarks often fail to capture failures caused by planning loops, tool use, component interactions, adaptive attacks, and system updates. A reusable scenario catalogue, reproducible attack artifacts, provenance-aware traces, and continuous reevaluation procedures could provide meaningful benefits to researchers, auditors, and engineering teams. The potential impact is reduced by uncertainty about whether adversarially discovered event rates can be translated into deployment risk and by the limited external validity of a catalogue tested on only two baseline architectures. Even so, the proposal addresses a timely gap with substantial practical relevance.

strengths: Strong alignment with architecture-aware agent evaluation and unusually comprehensive integration of scenarios, adaptive testing, reproducibility, provenance, and lifecycle reevaluation.

Concrete engineering deliverables and thoughtful experimental practices, including manifests, seedable attack oracles, ablations, power analysis, prior sensitivity checks, and reproducible failure artifacts.
Addresses a significant safety problem that is not adequately covered by static task benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central statistical comparison is not yet validly specified because adaptive-adversary and static i.i.d. evaluations sample different distributions, while selection effects, weighting, stopping rules, and multiple comparisons are not handled.

Key estimands and units are ambiguous, including the definition of an architecture-level violation, the meaning and allocation of N, and whether event rates represent adversarial detectability or deployment prevalence.
The full experiment is substantially over-scoped, and several peripheral components increase complexity without a clearly demonstrated contribution to the main hypothesis.
